title: Disease Monitoring Essentials
summary: Systematic evaluation of cancer response to treatment and detection of disease progression. Requires structured documentation using standardized criteria to guide clinical decisions.

content.text: Disease monitoring is the systematic process of assessing a patient's cancer status at defined intervals to determine treatment response, detect progression, and guide clinical decision-making. Standardized monitoring protocols ensure consistency in documentation and enable reliable communication across treatment teams.

items: Quantify tumor burden and measure change over time
Classify treatment response using standardized criteria (RECIST, PERCIST)
Detect disease progression or recurrence early
Guide decisions to continue, modify, or discontinue treatment
Document baseline disease status for prognostic assessment
Maintain consistent records for tumor boards and longitudinal tracking

content.text: Clear terminology prevents clinical errors in treatment planning. The following terms have distinct meanings and different prognostic implications.

items: Disease Progression: Increase in tumor burden on active treatment or within months of completing therapy
Recurrence: Reappearance of cancer after a complete response to prior treatment
Metastasis: Spread of cancer to a distant anatomic site (may be at diagnosis or develop later)
Treatment Resistance: Tumor growth despite adequate drug exposure; often indicates need for drug class change

content.text: Effective disease monitoring integrates three sources of information:
Radiologic evaluation of measurable disease using cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI) or metabolic imaging (PET). Provides objective measurement of tumor burden.
Serum or tissue markers that correlate with disease burden (e.g., CEA in colorectal cancer, PSA in prostate cancer, CA-125 in ovarian cancer). Supports and contextualizes imaging findings.
Patient symptoms, performance status changes, and physical examination findings. May indicate progression when imaging is stable or vice versa.
Monitoring intervals depend on cancer type, treatment phase, and clinical context. General principles:

items: During active therapy: Every 1-3 treatment cycles or every 6-12 weeks (varies by regimen)
After completion of therapy: Every 3-6 months for first 2 years, then every 6-12 months
If progression suspected: Urgent reassessment (days to 1 week) to confirm and guide next treatment
For hormone-sensitive cancers: May require less frequent monitoring if stable
Document baseline disease status (location, size, type of lesions)
Perform reassessment imaging at protocol-defined intervals
Measure changes in tumor burden (using RECIST or comparable criteria)
Classify response (CR, PR, SD, PD, or NE)
Correlate with biomarkers and clinical assessment
Document interpretation and clinical implications
Make treatment decision based on response category and overall clinical context
